strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine tension between unified joint diffusion (shared latent space) and causal diffusion (unidirectional conditioning), and positions a dual-stream design as a principled middle ground. Figure 1 effectively communicates this.

Consistent empirical gains across three distinct settings: simulation (RoboCasa, GR-1), real-world (Franka Research 3), and transfer learning (BridgeV2 pretraining), which collectively strengthen the central claim that world-model augmentation with modality decoupling helps.

The ablation in Table 6a is informative and cleanly isolates the two core design elements (dual-stream MMDiT vs. decoupled noising), showing both are necessary, with decoupled noise contributing more. The MMDiT depth and lambda_WM sweeps provide useful guidance.

The action-free video pretraining result (Table 4, 0.501 -> 0.585) is a meaningful demonstration that the architecture can absorb large-scale passive video, which is practically valuable and well aligned with the dual-stream design.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: architecture details, training hyperparameters, batch sizes, pseudocode for both training and test-time sampling, and an LLM-usage disclosure are provided.
weaknesses: No variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing is reported anywhere in the paper, despite real-world results being based on only 24 trials per task and test-time-scaling differences being on the order of 1-2 percentage points. Many reported gaps (e.g., Table 5 RoboCasa-100: 0.501 -> 0.504 -> 0.508 -> 0.518) are plausibly within run-to-run noise, which undermines the headline claim of a 2-6% test-time-scaling boost.

The closest related work, UWM (Zhu et al., 2025), is explicitly cited as using modality-specific time schedules yet is never compared against experimentally. Since UWM is arguably the most similar prior method, its absence materially weakens the originality and empirical positioning of the decoupled-noise contribution.

The core theoretical justification is asserted rather than demonstrated. The claim that the joint objective decomposes into a sum of unimodal flow-matching losses (Eq. 4, citing Rojas et al. 2025) is stated without proof or adaptation to this setting, and the narrative claims about learning forward/inverse causal relations from decoupled noise (Section 4.2) are not directly validated (e.g., no probe of whether the model actually recovers inverse dynamics).

Test-time scaling gains are non-monotonic and marginal (GR-1: 0.420 -> 0.451 -> 0.471 -> 0.450; RoboCasa-100 PnP actually drops at N_o=32), and no inference-latency or compute cost is quantified, so the practical value of the tunable efficiency/accuracy trade-off is unclear. The synchronous-sampling ablation (Table 7) partly justifies the async design but the framing is somewhat self-serving.

The FLARE baseline is a reimplementation (no official code), using DUST's own world-modeling target (SIGLIP embeddings) and an MLP aligner rather than the original Q-Former, so the FLARE comparison may not faithfully represent the original method; the paper acknowledges this but it limits the strength of the comparison.

Percentage reporting is inconsistent and potentially misleading: the abstract advertises 'up to 6% gains,' the introduction cites '5% and 6%,' and Section 5.1 claims '18% over GR00T-N1.5' for the same 100-demo setting (0.501 vs 0.417, i.e., ~8% absolute / ~20% relative). Mixing relative and absolute deltas without clarification makes the magnitude of improvement hard to interpret.

Real-world evaluation is limited to four pick-and-place tasks with a single robot and 60 demos each; generalization claims (e.g., 'robustness in physical environments and its promise for practical deployment') are broader than the evidence supports.

strengths: The dual-stream MMDiT architecture with per-modality AdaLN conditioning is a clean and reasonable design that directly targets the stated modality conflict (low-dimensional smooth actions vs. high-dimensional structured visual embeddings), and the paper is generally well-organized with helpful diagrams (Figs. 1-3).

The empirical evaluation spans three settings (RoboCasa, GR-1, real Franka Research 3), and the improvements are directionally consistent across benchmarks and demonstration scales (Tables 1-3). Real-world validation, while limited, is a genuine plus over purely simulated papers.

The real-world protocol is described carefully (predetermined configurations, half-success handling, four object categories per task), and the transfer-learning experiment with action-free BridgeV2 video (Table 4) is a valuable and promising direction.
Transparency is above average: detailed hyperparameters, batch sizes, iteration counts, pseudocode, and an explicit LLM-usage disclosure are provided, which aids partial reproducibility.
The ablation in Table 7 (naive synchronous step-scaling degrades performance) is a genuinely useful negative result that supports the claim that the asymmetry between modalities matters.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The core 'decoupled noise scheduling' is essentially independent per-modality noise injection, and the paper itself notes that UWM (Zhu et al., 2025) already 'extends this approach with modality-specific time schedules,' and that Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2025) already introduced independent per-token noise. The decomposition into a sum of unimodal losses is presented as a contribution but is a known result they attribute to Rojas et al. (2025). The MMDiT backbone is essentially the Stable Diffusion 3 architecture. The net contribution is an incremental recombination of existing ideas.

Missing comparisons to the most relevant baselines. PAD, EnerVerse, UWM, UVA, Video Policy, and VPP are discussed at length in Section 2 but never compared against. The only world-modeling baseline is a self-reimplemented FLARE (Section A.2) that drops the original Q-Former, making the comparison of questionable fidelity. This severely limits the strength of the central claim that DUST 'handles the modality conflict' better than alternatives.

No statistical rigor. No error bars, confidence intervals, or seeds are reported anywhere, despite robotics evaluations being notoriously high-variance. Several headline differences are small enough to be within noise (e.g., GR-1 300 demos: DUST 0.360 vs. FLARE 0.337; RoboCasa 1000 demos: 0.663 vs. 0.646), and the real-world evaluation uses only ~24 trials per task (Section A.4), which cannot support a 13% claim reliably.

Unsupported mechanistic claims. Figure 5 asserts that DUST 'leverages its internal prediction of future states by estimating where generated actions will position the gripper,' but there is no mechanism by which the parallel-generated vision stream corrects the action stream at inference, and no evidence is given for this causal story. It remains an anecdote rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

The world model itself is never quantitatively evaluated. There is no measurement of future-embedding prediction quality (e.g., MSE/alignment of predicted vs. actual SIGLIP-2 embeddings, or any planning-based use of the predicted future). The paper asserts that world modeling helps but only reports downstream success rates, so the link between the world-modeling objective and the gains is not established.

Test-time scaling results are weak and inconsistent with the claims. In Table 5 the RoboCasa 100-demo gain from 4->16 steps is 0.501->0.504 (0.3 points), GR-1 peaks non-monotonically at 32 steps (0.471) then drops at 64 (0.450), and the abstract's '6%' boost is inconsistent with the body's '2-5%'. No inference-time/compute accounting is provided for a method that multiplies vision steps up to 16x.

The transfer-learning experiment (Table 4) lacks the necessary control: it compares DUST-without-pretraining vs. DUST-with-pretraining but never reports GR00T/FLARE with the same BridgeV2 pretraining, so it is impossible to attribute the gain to DUST's dual-stream design rather than to video pretraining in general.

Internal inconsistencies and errors. The abstract says 'up to 6% gains over baseline methods,' while Section 5.1 reports 18% over GR00T and 5% over FLARE; the real-world gain is stated as both '13%' (abstract) and '12% over FLARE' (Section 5.1). Algorithm 2 contains a bug: the action update is placed inside the inner j-loop, updating the action every vision step (contradicting Eq. 5 and the text), and line 7 increments τ_A by Δτ_o rather than Δτ_A.

The ablation in Table 6a undercuts the architectural claim: MMDiT with joint noise (0.382) is essentially identical to plain DiT with joint noise (0.380), implying the dual-stream architecture provides no benefit on its own, and the interaction with decoupled noise is left unexplained. Similarly, λ_WM=1.0 (0.501) vs. 2.0 (0.496) and MMDiT depth results are all within noise, so the 'best' configurations are not convincingly identified.

There is no limitations section and no discussion of failure modes, computational cost, or negative results, despite the review criteria explicitly valuing honest treatment of limitations. The conclusion is purely promotional.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: modality conflict when jointly modeling actions and future observations in world-model-augmented VLA policies.

The dual-stream MMDiT architecture is clearly described and reasonably motivated: separate action/vision streams, shared cross-modal attention, modality-specific AdaLN, and modality-specific DiT refinement.

The decoupled noise schedule and per-modality flow-matching objective are simple and well aligned with the architecture; ablations in Table 6a show that decoupled noise provides a substantial gain over joint noise.
The empirical evaluation is broad, covering RoboCasa, GR-1, a real Franka Research 3 setup, transfer from action-free BridgeV2 video, and test-time scaling.
Real-world validation is valuable: Table 3 reports a 13 percentage-point average gain over GR00T-N1.5 and a 12-point gain over the reproduced FLARE baseline across four Franka pick-and-place tasks.
Transfer learning results in Table 4 are promising: BridgeV2 video pretraining improves RoboCasa 100-demo average success from 0.501 to 0.585.
The asynchronous test-time scaling is supported by a synchronous-step ablation (Table 7), which helps justify the claim that extra vision denoising steps are useful.
Reproducibility effort is nontrivial: the method builds on GR00T-N1.5, uses public simulation datasets, provides training hyperparameters and pseudocode, and includes an LLM-usage disclosure.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited. The MMDiT design with separate streams and shared attention closely resembles the MMDiT architecture from Stable Diffusion 3, which is not cited, while decoupled per-modality noise is closely related to Diffusion Forcing and UWM. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish DUST from UWM, which already uses modality-specific time schedules.

The evaluation omits direct comparisons to prior world-model-augmented VLA methods such as PAD, UWM, UVA, Video Policy, and Video Prediction Policy, despite citing them as closely related. The baselines are essentially GR00T-N1.5 and a reimplemented FLARE, which weakens the claim that DUST outperforms prior world-modeling approaches.

The FLARE baseline is not faithful to the original method: the authors replace its Q-Former with a small MLP and use DUST's world-modeling target. This may make FLARE artificially weak, so the reported FLARE comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

There is no statistical rigor. The paper reports no seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Real-world results are based on only 24 trials per task, so differences such as Task 3 (0.500 vs. 0.625) correspond to about three trials and may not be meaningful.

The sampling algorithm is technically inconsistent. In Eq. 5, the condition τ_A N_o mod q = 0 is always true if τ_A is advanced by Δτ_A = qΔτ_o, implying action updates every step rather than every q steps. Algorithm 2 also increments τ_A by Δτ_o but updates actions by Δτ_A on every inner loop, contradicting the stated asynchronous scheme.

The central theoretical justification cites 'Rojas et al. (2025),' but this reference does not appear in the bibliography. Moreover, decomposing the joint flow-matching loss into a sum of unimodal losses under independent noise injection is largely trivial and does not by itself establish the claimed causal dependencies.

The causality claims are overinterpreted. Independent per-modality timesteps and shared attention do not necessarily force the model to learn forward or inverse dynamics, and the paper provides no probing or quantitative evidence that such causal relationships are captured.

World-model quality is not evaluated. There are no metrics on future-embedding prediction accuracy, no comparison between predicted and actual future representations, and no analysis of whether or how the action stream actually uses the vision stream at inference.

Percentage reporting is inconsistent and sometimes misleading. The abstract says 'up to 6% gains,' while Table 1 shows an 8.4 percentage-point gain over GR00T-N1.5; Section 5.1 says 18% over GR00T and 5% over FLARE, whereas the table shows 8.4 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively. Percentage versus percentage-point usage is mixed throughout.

There is no limitations section. The paper does not discuss inference cost, failure modes, safety, compute requirements, or the lack of public release for the real-world data and code, which weakens reproducibility and responsible-claims treatment.

Several ablations rely on small differences without variance. For example, Table 6b shows 0.501 for 12 layers versus 0.493 for 14 layers, and Table 6c shows 0.501 for λ=1.0 versus 0.496 for λ=2.0; these differences may be within noise.

Transfer-learning experiments lack appropriate controls. There is no GR00T-N1.5 or FLARE baseline with the same BridgeV2 pretraining, so it is unclear whether the transfer gain is specific to DUST or would also appear with other world-modeling losses.

The claim that DUST avoids a unified latent space is overstated. Shared cross-modal attention still requires a common token dimension and enables substantial information exchange, so the distinction from a unified joint model is softer than presented.

There are minor presentation errors, including text references to 'Figure 6a-c' for ablation results that are actually in Table 6, and some equations omit expectations over the sampled noise and timesteps.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and well-motivated framework (DUST) that targets a real tension in world-model-augmented VLAs: the trade-off between cross-modal integration and modality-specific fidelity. The dual-stream MMDiT design with shared cross-modal attention is a sensible architectural resolution, and the decoupled per-modality noising is a natural and reasonable extension of diffusion forcing.

The experimental package is broad and convincing in scope: two simulated benchmarks (RoboCasa, GR-1), a real-world Franka Research 3 setup, plus LIBERO and CALVIN in the appendix. The inclusion of transfer-learning experiments (action-free BridgeV2 video pretraining and heterogeneous robot-human joint training with EgoDex) meaningfully strengthens the contribution beyond a single benchmark win.

The ablations (Table 7) are well-designed and isolate the two core components (dual-stream architecture and decoupled noise) plus sensitivity to MMDiT depth and the loss weight lambda_WM, providing evidence that both design elements contribute complementary gains. The inference-time benchmark (Figure 4) showing ~40Hz at 4 steps is a useful practical result.

The asynchronous sampling idea (Section 4.3, Table 6) is a clean, tunable mechanism, and the supporting ablation (Table 11) showing that synchronous step increases actually degrade performance provides good evidence that the decoupling—not just more steps—is responsible for the gains.
The failure-case analysis (Section A.11) and the zero-vision-step study (Table 13) are honest and informative, and the manuscript is generally well-organized with clear figures.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental. MMDiT-style dual streams with shared attention, per-modality noise (diffusion forcing), and per-modality flow-matching losses are all established ideas; the contribution is largely in combining and adapting them to the VLA setting. The 'causal relationship' framing overstates what is essentially independent noise injection at train time.

Statistical rigor is weak. No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed variance are reported anywhere, yet the key comparisons against the strongest baseline (FLARE) are small in simulation (e.g., RoboCasa 1000 demos: 66.3 vs 64.6; GR-1 1000 demos: 42.0 vs 36.3) and the real-world numbers rest on only 6 evaluations per task-object configuration. With margins this narrow and no variance estimates, it is difficult to assess whether the reported improvements are significant.

A reporting inconsistency raises concern about data integrity. The 'DUST + Video Pretrain' row in Table 5 (42.3 / 80.7 / 58.1, Avg 58.5) is numerically identical, to three subcategories, to the 'DUST, no mixture' row in Table 4 (42.3 / 80.7 / 58.1, Avg 58.5), even though these correspond to different data regimes (100-demo finetune with pretraining vs. 300-demo training without pretraining). The corresponding FLARE rows do differ, so this exact match is suspicious and needs clarification; if it is a copy error it undermines the pretraining claim in Table 5.

The FLARE baseline is a reimplementation (no released code/checkpoints), and the authors substitute their own SigLIP-2 world-modeling target and an MLP alignment module for FLARE's Q-Former design. While the stated goal is fairness, this reimplementation may not faithfully reproduce FLARE's behavior, making the head-to-head comparisons in Tables 1–5 and 3 somewhat uncertain. The same concern applies to PAD/VPP configurations.

Some presentation and consistency issues: the abstract states '2–5%' inference-scaling gains while Section 5.1 states '2–6%'; the text reports '5% and 6%' gains in the abstract but '18% over GR00T-N1.5 and 5% over FLARE' in the body; the reference list contains numerous year mismatches (e.g., Chen et al. 2024 vs 2025a, Li et al. 2023a vs 2025a, repeated 'Li et al. (2025)'), suggesting sloppiness.

Test-time scaling gains are marginal and non-monotonic (e.g., RoboCasa 100 demos 50.1 -> 51.8 at 64 steps; GR-1 regresses at 64 steps). The paper acknowledges this but the practical payoff of the mechanism remains modest given the added latency.
No code or checkpoints are mentioned for release (only a project page), which limits reproducibility given the reliance on reimplemented baselines.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem (augmenting VLAs with world modeling) and frames the trade-off between cross-modal integration and modality-specific fidelity clearly (Figure 1).

Broad empirical evaluation spanning two simulated benchmarks (RoboCasa, GR-1), two additional benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN in the appendix), real-world Franka experiments, and transfer-learning settings (action-free video pretraining, heterogeneous robot-human joint training).

Includes useful ablations: architecture vs. noise-schedule (Table 7a), MMDiT depth (7b), loss weight (7c), latent embedder choice (Table 8), synchronous vs. asynchronous scaling (Table 11), and an action-vision dependency probe (Table 12).
The asynchronous test-time scaling idea is sensible and the ablation in Table 11 makes a reasonable case that decoupling the number of denoising steps matters relative to naive synchronous scaling.
The MMDiT implementation details (Figure 5, independent AdaLN timestep embeddings per stream) are specified, and the inference-latency comparison (Figure 4) is a practically relevant addition.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty. The three core ingredients are all pre-existing: the MMDiT dual-stream design (Esser et al., 2024), decoupled/per-modality noise scheduling (explicitly 'inspired by diffusion forcing' and essentially the 'modality-specific time schedules' of UWM, Zhu et al., 2025), and the loss decomposition from Rojas et al. (2025). The paper does not clearly differentiate its contribution from UWM despite citing it, which undermines the originality claim of the decoupled training algorithm.

Weak support for the central architectural claim. In the decisive ablation (Table 7a), MMDiT with joint noise (38.2) is statistically indistinguishable from a plain single-stream DiT with joint noise (38.0). This suggests the dual-stream architecture by itself contributes essentially nothing, and the reported gains stem almost entirely from decoupled noise injection rather than the dual-stream design the paper is named for. The 'both components are indispensable' conclusion is not well supported by these numbers.

The explicit world-modeling at inference appears nearly irrelevant. In Table 13, running zero vision denoising steps at test time still yields 47.9% (vs. 50.1% default), which already exceeds both GR00T-N1.5 (41.7%) and FLARE (44.6%). This contradicts the narrative that 'explicit prediction allows DUST to anticipate where the gripper will land' and suggests the gains come from the training objective rather than the joint sampling/world-modeling mechanism.

Modest and inconsistent gains over the strongest baseline. Against the reproduced FLARE, DUST improves RoboCasa 1000-demo average from 64.6 to 66.3 (1.7%), GR-1 300-demo from 33.7 to 36.0 (2.3%), and on LIBERO the two are identical (96.2 vs. 96.2). The abstract's 'up to 6%' and '2-5% inference scaling' claims are drawn from favorable cells; many cells show flat or negative trends.

No statistical rigor. There are no confidence intervals, seed counts, or variance estimates anywhere, despite the paper making fine-grained comparative claims (e.g., 50.1 vs. 44.6, 59.9 vs. 49.5 on real-world tasks). Real-world results rest on 24 trials per task across 4 object configurations, which is too small to support the headline '>10%' claim without error bars.

Fairness of the key comparison. The strongest baseline (FLARE) is a re-implementation ('Because the FLARE implementation has not been released, we reimplemented it'), using a different alignment module (MLP instead of the original Q-Former). Since DUST's margins over FLARE are small, any weakness in this re-implementation could account for the difference. Likewise, π0/π0-FAST are initialized from PaliGemma rather than robot-pretrained checkpoints, making cross-method comparisons uneven.

Internal inconsistency between abstract/body and tables. The abstract claims 'up to 6% gains' and '2-5% improvement' from inference-time scaling, but Table 6 shows ~1.7-3% on RoboCasa and non-monotonic behavior on GR-1 (45.1 at 16 steps, 47.1 at 32, 45.0 at 64). The text acknowledges non-monotonicity but the headline framing overstates the effect.

Latent-target ablation undercuts the stated rationale. Table 8 shows SigLIP-2 (0.501), DINOv2 (0.516), and Flux.1 VAE (0.491) are essentially equivalent, with DINOv2 actually best. This weakens the paper's argument that semantic embedding targets are preferable to reconstructive latents; the choice appears not to matter much, and the discussion is not reconciled with this result.

Reproducibility gaps. Some equations are garbled or ambiguous: the beta schedule in Eq. 1 ('τ∼Beta((s-τ)/τ;1.5,1.0)') is malformed, and the action-update condition in Eq. 5 ('τ_A N_o mod q = 0') is unclear. Training regimes are highly inconsistent (60k steps for 100 demos, 420k for 300, 600k for 1000; 960 batch on 8×H200 for GR-1), which complicates independent reproduction and raises questions about whether baselines received comparable tuning.

The '3-10× faster' inference claim conflicts with the fact that GR-1 training required a 960 global batch on 8 H200s and the paper's own scaling results show latency climbing to 246 ms (Figure 4) at higher step counts; the efficiency story is presented selectively.

The failure analysis (A.11) is honest but reveals that DUST's core mechanism (future visual prediction) is precisely what makes it brittle under occlusion, which is not addressed in the method itself beyond speculative future directions.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: integrating world modeling into VLA policies and resolving the trade-off between unified joint diffusion and causal separate models. The dual-stream MMDiT design is a sensible solution that maintains modality-specific processing while enabling cross-modal exchange.

The decoupled noise scheduling and per-modality flow matching loss are well-motivated and supported by ablations: on RoboCasa with 100 demos, MMDiT+decoupled noise reaches 50.1% vs 38.2% for MMDiT+joint noise and 42.5% for DiT+decoupled, showing both components contribute.

Extensive empirical evaluation: simulated benchmarks (RoboCasa, GR-1, plus LIBERO and CALVIN in the appendix), real-world Franka Research 3 tasks, transfer learning (action-free video pretraining and heterogeneous joint training), test-time scaling, and component ablations. This breadth is impressive.

Strong and consistent results across most settings: e.g., RoboCasa 100 demos 50.1% vs 41.7% (GR00T-N1.5) and 44.6% (FLARE); GR-1 1000 demos 42.0% vs 30.8% and 36.3%; real-world 59.9% vs 46.5% and 49.5%. Gains are especially notable in low-data regimes and real-world tasks.

The asynchronous joint sampling strategy is novel and validated: increasing vision denoising steps while fixing action steps yields gains (e.g., GR-1 1000 demos 42.0% to 47.1% at N_o=32), whereas synchronous step increases degrade performance (Table 11), supporting the design choice.

Transfer learning results are valuable: action-free BridgeV2 video pretraining improves DUST from 50.1% to 58.5% on RoboCasa 100 demos, and joint training with GR-1 and EgoDex improves from 58.5% to 64.4%, showing scalability to heterogeneous data.
Inference efficiency is competitive: DUST with 4 steps runs at ~40Hz, faster than π0 (~13Hz), π0-FAST (~3Hz), and OpenVLA (~5.5Hz), making it practical for closed-loop control.

Reproducibility is generally good: public benchmarks, detailed training hyperparameters, GPU configurations, architecture details, and baseline reimplementation notes. The failure case analysis (A.11) and non-monotonic scaling discussion show honest limitations.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the decoupled loss is asserted rather than derived. The claim that the joint objective decomposes into a sum of unimodal losses given independent noise injection (Eq. 4) is nontrivial and may not hold when the network conditions on both modalities. The paper cites Rojas et al. (2025) without explaining the required conditions, which could mislead readers. The empirical results still support the method, but the theoretical framing needs clarification.

Eq. 5's asynchronous sampling condition appears incorrect: 'if (τ_A N_o mod q = 0)' will almost always be true once action timesteps are multiples of qΔτ_o, contradicting the described 'update every q steps.' The intended condition should depend on the global step index (e.g., n mod q = 0). This is a technical/presentational error that should be fixed.

The evaluation lacks statistical significance and error bars, especially for real-world experiments (24 trials per task). Differences such as 59.9% vs 49.5% could be within noise. Reporting confidence intervals or multiple seeds would strengthen the claims.

Baseline comparisons have caveats: FLARE is reimplemented without its original Q-Former, π0 and π0-FAST are initialized from PaliGemma rather than robot-pretrained checkpoints, and GR00T-N1.5 uses a randomly initialized action expert. These choices may disadvantage baselines and do not fully reflect state-of-the-art performance, so the 'state-of-the-art' claims should be tempered.

The improvement over the strongest baseline (FLARE) is modest in several simulation settings (e.g., RoboCasa 1000: +1.7%, GR-1 300: +2.3%, LIBERO: tie), although gains over GR00T-N1.5 and in real-world/transfer settings are larger. This raises questions about the incremental benefit of the proposed architecture over implicit world modeling.

The world model predicts a single future embedding rather than a multi-step future trajectory or explicit video, limiting the scope of 'world modeling.' At inference, the zero-vision-denoising ablation (Table 13) shows that explicit future prediction contributes only ~2.2% average gain, suggesting the main benefits come from the training objective rather than test-time world-model usage.

The paper does not compare against closely related unified world-model methods such as UWM (Zhu et al., 2025), which also uses modality-specific time schedules. This would help position DUST's novelty and effectiveness.

Some implementation details are missing or unclear: the distribution for sampling τ_o is not specified, the action noise distribution in Eq. 1 has a suspicious Beta parameterization, and the MMDiT modification (Figure 5) could be described more precisely. These minor issues affect reproducibility.

The limitations discussion is largely confined to appendix A.11 and the non-monotonic scaling paragraph. A dedicated limitations section in the main text would better contextualize when DUST is expected to fail (e.g., occlusion, visual noise) and the computational cost of test-time scaling.
